articles.title: 16 Ecuadorian fishermen sue US government, allege drone attack destroyed their boat near the Galápagos
articles.summary: Ecuadorian fishermen allege U.S. drones struck their boat in the Pacific Ocean near the Galápagos, forcing the crew to jump overboard, a lawsuit says.
articles.body: More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen have sued the federal government, alleging they were wrongly targeted in a drone strike that destroyed their boat in the Pacific Ocean earlier this year as part of the Trump administration’s broader campaign against vessels suspected of drug trafficking. The 16 fishermen aboard La Negra Francisca Duarte II say drones launched from a U.S. vessel struck their boat March 17, 2026, as they headed home from a two-week fishing trip near the Galápagos. The strike set the boat ablaze, forcing the crew to jump overboard and escape in lifeboats, according to a lawsuit filed Monday in federal court in Pennsylvania. All 16 survived, but two suffered serious burns. One man’s leg was burned to the bone, the lawsuit says. The fishermen’s lawyers say the crew had no ties to drug cartels or terrorist groups and posed no imminent threat when U.S. drones struck their vessel, which they say had been cleared by Ecuadorian authorities hours earlier. US MILITARY LAUNCHES FIRST AUTONOMOUS WARFARE COMMAND TO DEPLOY UNMANNED SYSTEMS ACROSS LATIN AMERICA After their boat was destroyed, the fishermen sailed toward a blue vessel, which the lawsuit identified as a U.S. ship. Some personnel wore U.S. Coast Guard vests, the suit says. They allegedly zip-tied the uninjured men, hooded them and forced them to stand barefoot on the hot metal deck with no food and little water. One injured fisherman was taken below deck for treatment, where U.S. personnel allegedly told him they had carried out the drone strike and laughed about destroying the boat, according to the lawsuit. The fishermen were held until the next day before they were put on an El Salvadoran ship that took them back to El Salvador, where they were held at a migrant center in "deplorable conditions" until the end of March. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN The Department of War and the U.S. Coast Guard have denied knowing about or being involved in the March 17 attack on La Negra Francisca Duarte II. U.S. Southern Command declined to comment, citing its policy of not issuing statements on pending or ongoing litigation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The lawsuit argues that the Trump administration’s strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific violate federal and international law because they have been carried out outside an armed conflict. It adds that even if an armed conflict existed, the attacks could constitute war crimes under the Geneva Conventions. The plaintiffs are seeking compensatory and other financial damages to be determined at trial, plus an injunction ordering the U.S. to end similar boat attacks.

articles.title: Senate Republicans advance Trump's effort to abolish Dept of Education
articles.summary: Senate Republicans, led by Jim Banks, push a 10-bill package to permanently transfer Department of Education programs, codifying Trump's dismantling order.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Senate Republicans are advancing a major legislative push to dismantle the Department of Education, introducing a 10-bill package aimed at permanently transferring the agency’s core programs to other federal departments. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., introduced the Senate companion to the Less Bureaucracy, Better Education legislative package on Wednesday, which would codify President Donald Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon’s executive actions to wind down the department. Sens. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., and Ashley Moody, R-Fla., are co-sponsoring the Senate effort. "The federal education bureaucracy has failed students and families for decades. President Trump and Secretary McMahon are finally putting parents first and returning power where it belongs. Our bills will make their reforms permanent, eliminate layers of Washington bureaucracy and ensure taxpayers are no longer forced to prop up a failed department," Banks told Fox News Digital. DEPT OF ED PUSHES AHEAD WITH EFFORTS TO DISMANTLE FEDERAL BUREAUCRACY AFTER BLUE WAVE Throughout his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump promised to eliminate the Department of Education, later signing a March 2025 executive order directing McMahon to begin dismantling the 45-year-old agency. While fully abolishing a Cabinet-level department requires congressional approval — and 60 votes to overcome a Senate filibuster — Republicans are moving to lock in the administration's restructuring piece by piece. McMahon told Fox News Digital that the department acts primarily as a pass-through entity for federal dollars and contends that its day-to-day operations are nonessential. "For too long, an overgrown Washington bureaucracy has funneled trillions of taxpayer dollars into top-down mandates and administrative red tape. Exactly one year after we announced six critical partnerships to begin reversing that trend, Senators Banks, Tuberville, Moody and Lee are introducing the ‘Less Bureaucracy, Better Education’ package to permanently codify the Trump Administration’s historic reforms," she said. She went on to say, "This vital legislation will make permanent the work we have done to align programs with the agencies best suited to support them and return education authority to those closest to the child. I commend their leadership in launching this important effort, and I look forward to working together to improve education for our students and families." The Senate introduction follows 10 interagency agreements signed between May 2025 and March 2026 across five federal departments — Labor, Treasury, Health and Human Services, State and Interior — as the Education Department seeks to shrink its footprint. TRUMP’S FIRST-YEAR GOVERNMENT OVERHAUL DELIVERS CHANGE WASHINGTON HASN’T SEEN SINCE THE 1960S For example, the Department of Labor took on a major role in the day-to-day administration of adult education, family literacy and career and technical education programs under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act and the Perkins Act. While Labor manages operational duties, the Department of Education retains statutory oversight as services shift to states and grant recipients. In another major move, the agency partnered with the Department of the Treasury to assume operational responsibility for managing the federal student loan portfolio and collecting on defaulted student debt. MCMAHON CALLS FOR 'RESET' OF EDUCATION AFTER US SPENT $3 TRILLION AND STILL SAW READING SCORES DECLINE According to Department of Education officials, the goal of the partnerships is to demonstrate a "proof of concept" to Congress that essential federal education functions and funding flows can be reallocated across executive branch agencies without disruption. An agency official previously told Fox News Digital that staffers are effectively working to put themselves out of a job under Trump's orders because the department is unnecessary. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS ‘HARD RESET’ FOR AMERICAN SCHOOLS, VOWS TO PUT PARENTS ‘BACK IN CHARGE’ The House Education and Workforce Committee, led by Chairman Tim Walberg, R-Mich., already advanced its version of the 10-bill package along party lines in July. "Every student deserves an education that works for them, yet the status quo is failing our children. Republicans believe in a new vision that puts students, families and educators in the driver’s seat. I am glad to see my colleagues in the Senate take action to end the bureaucracy and deliver on that vision for the American people," Walberg told Fox News Digital. CHARTER SCHOOL FOUNDER BACKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PUSH TO DECENTRALIZE K-12 EDUCATION Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, echoed that sentiment, arguing that Washington has sidelined local communities for too long. "For too long, the centralized bureaucracy of the Department of Education has overridden state and local control of schooling while failing America’s families. As President Trump returns education to the people, our legislation returns the remaining worthwhile function of the Department to other appropriate federal agencies," Lee told Fox News Digital. The Education Department announced earlier this year it moved to a smaller building to reduce the agency's footprint as part of its broader effort to dismantle itself. Department staff will move out of the Lyndon B. Johnson headquarters building, so the Department of Energy can eventually move in by August. "Our schools are supposed to be preparing the next generation of Americans for LIFE — not pushing some woke ideology. I’m proud to introduce this bill with Sen. Banks to codify one of President Trump’s biggest promises — dismantling the [ED]. Let’s put our students first and get it done," Sen. Tuberville told Fox News Digital. articles.title: These 7 newly elected Democrats voted against Jeffries for House Speaker
articles.summary: A bloc of seven incoming House Democrats voted against Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) being the next Speaker in an internal caucus vote Wednesday. The seven Democrats then made their votes known in a joint statement. They were among 11 votes against Jeffries in the internal vote. Jeffries’s bid was supported by 251 lawmakers. The seven…
articles.body:
A bloc of seven incoming House Democrats voted against Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) being the next Speaker in an internal caucus vote Wednesday.

The seven Democrats then made their votes known in a joint statement. They were among 11 votes against Jeffries in the internal vote. Jeffries’s bid was supported by 251 lawmakers.

The seven who voted against Jeffries and made their views public were Democratic Rep.-elects Darializa Avila Chevalier (N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (N.J.), Frederick Haynes (Texas), Melat Kiros (Colo.), Donavan McKinney (Mich.), Chris Rabb (Pa.) and Claire Valdez (N.Y.).

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the group wrote in a statement.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations,” they continued. “While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership.”

“Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” the bloc concluded.

Five of the members who voted against Jeffries and signed the statement were backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which made waves this election cycle for its progressive stances.

Newly elected DSA lawmakers were expected to create headaches for Jeffries as the group reportedly remained divided on how to approach changing the Democratic party’s stances. They’ve hammered their own party for what they see as an abandonment of progressive ideals and a soft-glove approach to President Trump’s second term.

Kiros’s race in Colorado drew national attention after she ousted 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.). She ran on securing universal childcare and eldercare and supported an ultramillionaire tax on people with a net worth of more than $50 million.

Others in the group ran on similar platforms, overthrowing long-term centrist incumbents.

Nomiki Konst, a progressive strategist who is an inactive member of the DSA, predicted in October that most of the left in the caucus are going to side with Jeffries, noting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) struggles against then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.)

The new DSA congressional members “have learned the lessons” of Ocasio-Cortez, Konst told The Hill.

Still their lack of support marks a new challenge that Jeffries will be expected to handle as division between centrists and progressives within the party continues to grow.

Hamawy and Haynes are not affiliated or a part of the DSA but campaigned on progressive platforms.

A spokesperson for Haynes shared a statement with Time that the incoming lawmaker ‘woke up unexpectedly ill this morning” and “narrowly missed the vote.” His team shared that if he did cast his vote, Haynes would have voted against Jeffries becoming House Speaker.

Haynes is replacing outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett’s (D-Texas) open House seat after her failed bid for Texas’s Senate seat. He differed from Crockett who voted to send U.S. military to Israel.

Christ was against genocide and that if “it’s in Gaza, he’s against it,” he told Texas outlet WFAA .

While Hamawy, a doctor and veteran, took hold of outgoing Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman’s (D-N.J.) seat who served in the House since 2015. On the campaign trail, he wouldn’t commit to backing Jeffries, telling the New Jersey Globe that current Democratic leadership is “failing to meet the moment.”

articles.title: Ron Johnson: Remark about shutting down Social Security was ‘imprecise’
articles.summary: Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, said there is “no way to fix” Social Security, calling for it to be shut down, but later clarified that his comments were “imprecise.” “At this point, there’s really no way to fix Social Security. It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it, you just…
articles.body:
Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), who chairs the Senate Budget Committee , said there is “no way to fix” Social Security, calling for it to be shut down, but later clarified that his comments were “imprecise.”

“At this point, there’s really no way to fix Social Security. It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it, you just shut it down and hope that you can recover some of your money,” Johnson said during an appearance on Fox Business .

During a Senate committee hearing to examine Social Security, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) questioned Johnson’s remarks saying, “This is the first time in decades that a senior senator, the chairman of the Budget Committee, said he would rather shut down Social Security than fix it.”

“Social Security does have to evolve to meet the challenges,” Wyden said.

“This proposition of throwing in the towel folks which is what we heard … I think would be a huge mistake,” he added. “I think the American people would say we sent you there to roll up your sleeves and fix the problem not quit on it.”

Johnson responded by saying, “I was talking about Ponzi schemes … imprecise statement I’ll admit but everything I’ve written everything I’ve said clearly I’m not proposing shutting down Social Security.”

Earlier this month, Wyden said there is a “ lot of interest ” among lawmakers to raise the Social Security payroll tax cap. In 2026, the wage base limit for Social Security taxes $184,500 in income, according to the Internal Revenue Service website .

“The wage base limit is the maximum wage that’s subject to the tax for that year,” the website says. However, for Medicare, the base limit does not exist.

In June, Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) backed raising the Social Security tax cap in a New York Times opinion piece .

“This is a no-brainer: The wealthiest Americans, who have benefited the most from America’s opportunities, should contribute the same percentage of their income as a factory worker in Chillicothe, Ohio, or a teacher in Worcester, Mass.,” they wrote.

articles.title: Protesters heckle Trump's ex-Border Patrol chief offstage after Dem governor condemns College Republican event
articles.summary: Protesters shouted "Immigrants are welcome here" as Gregory Bovino was escorted offstage at Rutgers College Republicans event Mikie Sherrill called "wrong."
articles.body: Protesters heckled former Trump Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino off stage during a Monday night speech at Rutgers University, hours after New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill called the Rutgers College Republicans’ decision to host him "wrong" and urged the club to reconsider. Bovino previously criticized Sherrill online, accusing her of prioritizing illegal immigrants over New Jersey residents. After returning to the stage, he called her "Sugar Pop Sherrill" and "Kim Jong Sherrill." Speaking to reporters afterward, he said she wanted to "trounce this freedom of speech," described the "Kim Jong Sherrill" label as "very fitting" and called the governor a "totalitarian." He also told Blaze News that Sherrill had timed her social media comments to "foment violence" against conservatives. At Monday night’s Rutgers College Republicans event, protesters began shouting within minutes of Bovino taking the stage. Rutgers police escorted him offstage and ordered the hecklers to leave or face arrest, according to local reports. Bovino returned about ten minutes later to resume his remarks and answer questions. Hundreds of protesters also gathered outside. 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS "What’s so crazy is that you all allowed a Nazi to be here," a protester yelled as the heckling began. Another shouted, "Your fascist death cult is failing!" Video from inside the event captured chants of "Get out of New Jersey!" and "Immigrants are welcome here!" Outside, hundreds of protesters carried images of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed by federal agents in Minneapolis. Before Bovino’s Monday appearance, Rutgers told Fox News Digital it was committed to protecting freedom of expression and maintaining campus security. The university also said hosting a student-organized event did not constitute an endorsement of the speaker or his views. Rutgers had not responded to Fox News Digital's follow-up request for comment about the disruption by publication. Hours before Bovino’s speech, Sherrill said in a social media post that she was "deeply disappointed" by the Rutgers College Republicans’ invitation, adding, "Giving him a platform is the wrong decision." Sherrill said that if the club went ahead with the event, she would ensure the state worked with Rutgers to protect "the safety of everyone and the rights enshrined in our Constitution," and she urged attendees to question Bovino about his record. SHERRILL COMMITS $20.2M TO DEPORTATION DEFENSE WHILE CONDEMNING RUTGERS OVER BORDER PATROL SPEAKER Fox News Digital contacted Sherrill's team for comment on the disruption at Bovino’s event but received no response before publication. Bovino served as Trump's commander-at-large of the U.S. Border Patrol and oversaw immigration enforcement and deportation operations, including Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis. He was removed from command in January following the shootings of Good and Pretti and retired from the Border Patrol in March. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP During the Rutgers College Republicans event, a student asked Bovino about the deaths of Good and Pretti. He replied, "Poor decisions come with consequences," then said the circumstances were "still being sorted out." Bovino called ICE agents the "real victims" and added, "I love them and salute them." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Asked after Monday’s event whether he stood by the deaths of Pretti and Good, Bovino said, "I didn’t stand by anybody’s death." He clarified that his earlier comment about going "harder" referred to mass deportation operations, not the shootings of Good or Pretti. Bovino said he would rejoin the Border Patrol "in an instant" to continue those operations and called the end of enforcement activity in Minnesota "the great surrender." He added that he hoped the administration would complete its mass deportation efforts but feared it would "surrender" its aggressive deportation agenda.

articles.title: Californians sound off on Newsom’s death penalty move, midterms and failed billionaire tax
articles.summary: Los Angeles locals share their takes on California’s biggest political flashpoints, from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s death row commutations to the billionaire tax and Democrats’ next moves.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — From California Gov. Gavin Newsom's decision to commute hundreds of death sentences to the defeat of a proposed billionaire tax, the state's biggest political controversies have sparked sharply divided reactions. With Democrats preparing to take control of Congress in January, Californians also have strong opinions about what the party should prioritize, from healthcare and affordability to releasing the Epstein files and investigating the Trump administration. Fox News Digital hit the streets of Los Angeles to hear directly from locals who offered blunt assessments of the issues shaping California’s political landscape and the country’s next chapter. GAVIN NEWSOM WIPES OUT CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW IN HISTORIC MASS COMMUTATION Newsom’s death penalty commutations draw split reactions Gavin Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he planned to commute all 548 of California's death sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole. California has not executed an inmate since 2006, and voters in the state have previously rejected proposals seeking to abolish the death penalty. Newsom maintains, however, that California "cannot morally kill" those on death row. Dozens of California district attorneys have sued to challenge Newsom's clemency. The decision has drawn mixed reactions, with some victims' families expressing support while others, along with prosecutors, have strongly opposed the move. Critics question how the governor could spare the lives of inmates convicted of carrying out some of the nation’s most brutal homicides. Fox News Digital asked people in Los Angeles whether they support Newsom's death penalty commutations. Some voiced support for the move, questioning the death penalty's constitutionality. "I'm OK with that. ... I don't think you need to kill anyone. They can die in prison. That's fine," Los Angeles resident Lawrence said. "One hundred percent," Milan of Los Angeles said. "I think death row should be abolished entirely. CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE' "Anyone on death row should have the chance to continue the rehabilitation because the whole point of our judicial system and jail system in the whole first place was for people who did something wrong to be rehabilitated, to go back into society," she added. "To be honest, yeah," Los Angeles local Sam said in support of Gov. Newsom’s commutations. "I think it's worse to spend your whole life in jail, so if you really want to punish somebody, then probably life in prison without parole is worse than the death penalty." "I'm not really sure. It depends on the level of the crime," Los Angeles resident Zoe said. "To me, being in prison forever would be worse than being put to death. So, for me, I'd rather them suffer for the rest of their life." Others, however, defended capital punishment for those convicted of serious crimes, including murder. "I'm for capital punishment," Dave of Santa Monica told Fox News Digital. "I think [Newsom] should stick with the federal guidelines around capital punishment," Los Angeles local David told Fox News Digital. "If you are proven beyond a reasonable doubt to be guilty of murder, there's probably only one way to handle that." What Californians want Democrats to tackle first California was among the states that helped fuel a nationwide Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections, with Democrats flipping five Republican-held House seats in the state and contributing to the party's takeover of Congress. The gains followed California voters' approval of Proposition 50 in 2025, which redrew congressional districts to favor Democrats in response to Republican-backed redistricting efforts in Texas. California voters spoke with Fox News Digital about how they voted and which policies they want the Democratic majority to tackle first when they assume office in January. One Los Angeles resident said the first thing on his list is the Epstein files, and another said she would like Democrats to halt U.S. involvement with the war in Iran. "Epstein files," said Sam. "Just the fact that all this is being swept under the rug for so long. We pay taxes. Rich people, billionaires don't pay taxes. The whole system's f---ed up. It's bulls---. The only way to fix it is to burn everything down, like a house with a bad foundation." "Stopping all of the illegal actions that are taking place, things that were supposed to have congressional approval. They should, those should be stopped," said Zoe, referring to U.S. military action involving Iran. "Wars, dropping bombs on people." DEMS' CALIFORNIA REDISTRICTING MASTERMIND FLIPS SCRIPT AFTER HELPING PARTY WIN 5 GOP SEATS: 'KILL' Healthcare also emerged as a top priority for California Democrats. "One thing and one thing only: healthcare," said David, adding he voted for candidates on the "left side." "Healthcare for all," Lawrence said. When asked by Fox News Digital how such a program would be funded, he responded, "Taxing those that have the most amount and are doing incredibly well in this country. Taxing them a little bit more isn't going to hurt them." Other Californians said they want Republicans and Democrats to work across the aisle and focus on collaboration over partisan clashes. "I hope that their first, like, publicity goal, in a sense, is to take out that separation of far right and far left, because there should just be like a purple in a sense," Milan said. "I would like them to work with the Republicans and the president," Dave told Fox News Digital. When asked if he thought they would, he responded, "No, I don't." Los Angeles locals react to billionaire tax defeat One of the most watched measures on California’s 2026 midterm ballot was Proposition 40's billionaire tax, a proposed one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to generate $100 billion for healthcare and education. California voters rejected the proposal, with roughly 53% voting against it and 47% supporting it, according to The Associated Press. Its defeat marked a blow for progressives that had championed taxing the state's wealthiest residents. California's wealthy technology executives poured millions of dollars into political action committees to defeat Prop 40, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who spent over $100 million. Gov. Newsom notably opposed the measure and implored his constituents to follow suit. Several Los Angeles residents questioned why the wealth tax failed in heavily Democratic California, with one attributing its defeat to "propaganda." "I think that's crazy. I think it was like over a few million votes for it. I know there's not a few billion billionaires who voted. So, I think it's due to propaganda," Milan said. DEMOCRATS SET SIGHTS ON ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER MIDTERM WINS, BUT PRITZKER DRAWS A SURPRISING LINE "That was a surprise. I don't know how many billionaires there are in California but ... it's less than 1%, and, so, I'm very surprised it didn't pass," Lawrence said. "I don't know who voted for that." "That sucks, to be honest," said Sam. "If these billionaires can get away with not paying taxes and me or anybody else has to pay their taxes basically on a middle class or lower income salary, I think it's f---ing disgusting, honestly. And I think these people should be taxed, 100%. I mean, the wealth gap here is insane. Like, the inequalities between the haves and the have nots." Others welcomed the proposal's defeat, arguing that imposing additional taxes on billionaires could drive wealthy residents out of California and hurt the state's economy. "I don't want the billionaires to leave California," Zoe countered. "That's good that that failed for the sake of the economy of California. ... I mean, they’re the ones paying most of the taxes, right?" Dave told Fox News Digital. Should Democrats prioritize affordability or Trump probes? Democrats are expected to launch several investigations into President Donald Trump, his Cabinet and business allies once they assume the congressional majority in January. Top House and Senate Democrats told Fox News Digital they are considering investigations, congressional hearings and potential impeachment proceedings targeting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan. Republicans have characterized Democrats’ planned proceedings against Trump officials as politically motivated, and the administration has already shown it is prepared to push back against congressional investigations. Fox News Digital asked Los Angeles residents whether they would prefer Democrats to prioritize affordability and other issues affecting Americans or focus on investigating the Trump administration. "They can do both. They can walk and chew gum at the same time," said Lawrence. "If it's easy stuff that isn't going to take time out of doing what needs to be done to help the people, I would say go for it," Zoe told Fox News Digital. Several Los Angeles residents argued that Democrats should prioritize issues directly affecting everyday Americans but also acknowledged the importance of holding the Trump administration accountable. "Both are necessary, but I think most people are much more concerned with healthcare than they are about holding anyone responsible, although I think both are important," David said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The daily citizen matters a lot more than this drawn-on fight that is going to happen," said Milan. "This fight matters very much to hold the Trump administration accountable. They need to be held accountable, but that is gonna take a long time and a lot of back and forth." Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth visits Venezuela with focus on strengthening military partnership
articles.summary: President Delcy Rodríguez said in remarks with Hegseth that cooperation agreements between the two nations will allow the U.S. to offer training to Venezuela’s armed forces.
articles.body: CARACAS, Venezuela — U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is visiting Venezuela to meet with interim authorities on Wednesday, underscoring efforts by President Donald Trump’s administration to deepen its influence in the South American country since U.S. forces ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro in January. Hegseth is the latest member of Trump’s Cabinet to travel to Venezuela following visits this year by the Interior and Energy secretaries, who have focused on efforts to tap its oil reserves and critical minerals. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves. Venezuelan state television broadcast footage of Hegseth at the presidential palace in Caracas, alongside acting President Delcy Rodríguez. Hegseth, whose visit was not publicly announced by the Pentagon, is there months after American forces carried out a surprise nighttime raid in the Venezuelan capital to capture Maduro and whisk him to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Maduro has denied the accusations in U.S. court. Rodríguez, in televised remarks with Hegseth, said cooperation agreements between their nations will allow the U.S. to offer training to Venezuela’s armed forces. “The possibility again to strengthen the training of our Bolivarian National Armed Force, to favor its operational equipment, to facilitate access to new technologies is very beneficial for our military officials,” she said, adding that the training will allow the countries to “face common threats.” Hegseth said he looked forward to deepening the military partnership between the two countries and working together to fight drug smuggling. “We spent some time talking about the long history of our countries, so in many ways we see this as a reestablishment of our defense partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries,” he said. The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year. The U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump returned to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels. To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs. Hegseth’s visit comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years. Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture. Rodríguez’s court-allowed term expired in July, but she continues to function as Venezuela’s head of state. Opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by his country, which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy. The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country. The Trump administration says it has returned more than $12 billion, or almost 99%, of the revenue obtained from the sales of Venezuelan oil back to the country under the terms of the energy deal reached with Rodríguez’s government, according to a report released this month.

articles.title: Nike pledges free sneakers to every high school valedictorian after Colom request
articles.summary: Nike has promised to give free sneakers to high school valedictorians across the U.S. in the 2026-27 school year after Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D) asked the company to reward top-performing students in his home state to celebrate his historic midterm election victory. Colom, who became the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the…
articles.body:
Nike has promised to give free sneakers to high school valedictorians across the U.S. in the 2026-27 school year after Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D) asked the company to reward top-performing students in his home state to celebrate his historic midterm election victory.

Colom, who became the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era, initially made a proposal to Nike on social media: to give a pair of custom-made Air Force 1 sneakers to every high school valedictorian in Mississippi.

“To honor this moment in Mississippi history, how about custom-made AF1s (my fav shoe) for every valedictorian of Mississippi high school this year?” Colom wrote on Monday on the social platform X , tagging the sportswear giant in the post. “It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year!”

Nike responded Tuesday with an even bigger offer, announcing that it would expand the giveaway to include valedictorians nationwide.

“The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea,” Nike’s official X account wrote in response to Colom’s post. “We’ll do you one better… For this year, 2026/2027 high school valedictorians from across the U.S., let’s go! Stay tuned for more info.”

Colom praised Nike for embracing the idea and suggested Nike pay tribute to Hiram Revels in its custom design, who became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870 when he represented Mississippi during the Reconstruction era.

“I’m so proud of @Nike for stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment. This is the #justdoit mentality that makes your company great,” Colom wrote , referencing Nike’s slogan.

Colom defeated Trump-backed incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) in a shock upset in Mississippi’s closely watched Senate race earlier this month, becoming the first Black candidate elected to represent the state in the Senate in more than 150 years.

Hyde-Smith was favored to win the seat in a state that had not sent a Democrat to the Senate since John Stennis in 1982. Colom’s victory in Mississippi was one of several historic wins for Democrats in this year’s midterm elections. Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) became the first Black woman to serve as Georgia’s governor and Texas elected Gina Hinojosa (D) as its first Latina governor.

articles.title: Republican Senator Cornyn blocks Trump judicial nominee in Texas
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's efforts to secure Senate confirmation of as many conservative judges as possible before Democrats...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's efforts to secure Senate confirmation of as many conservative judges as possible before Democrats take control of the chamber suffered a setback on Wednesday after ‌a Republican senator blocked one of his nominees from advancing.

Outgoing Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas withheld support for US ‌Department of Justice official T. Elliot Gaiser to appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee for a hearing on Wednesday where it could take up his nomination to be a ​federal judge in Dallas.

Cornyn's decision not to return a so-called blue slip backing Gaiser marked the latest instance of a Republican senator not supporting a White House-backed judicial nominee in their home state during the lame-duck session before Democrats take control of the Senate on January 3.

"He's not from Texas," Cornyn told Reuters. "He has no trial experience, and the White House was trying to jam him down our throat without adequate ‌vetting for a lifetime job."

A White House official ⁠in a statement said it expects all of Trump's judicial nominees to be confirmed by year's end.

Senators traditionally help choose nominees for vacancies on federal courts in their states. By Senate custom, they can effectively veto ⁠trial court nominees they oppose in their states by refusing to return a blue slip, a form used to signal support.

Trump nominated Gaiser, 37, to a seat on the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas after the election.

The former Ohio solicitor general previously clerked for conservative US ​Supreme ​Court Justice Samuel Alito and currently heads the Justice Department's Office of ​Legal Counsel, a key unit that has frequently signed ‌off on the legality of his administration's actions.

Cornyn, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, during Wednesday's hearing expressed support for Trump's decision to separately nominate Texas Supreme Court Justice James Sullivan to serve as a federal judge after he was defeated by a Democrat in the recent election.

But Cornyn has been pushing for the White House to pick someone else for the seat Gaiser was nominated to fill, recommending instead former federal prosecutor Steve Fahey of Texas.

"And the White House now seems to ‌be showing some interest in that," Cornyn said in an interview.

Republican Senator Ted ​Cruz of Texas, who supports Gaiser, in a statement warned that the White ​House has indicated that it would be "impossible for a brand-new ​nominee to complete the FBI background check fast enough to be confirmed."

"If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not ‌move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay ​the price because it will effectively ​give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity," Cruz said.

Two of Trump's other judicial nominees similarly ran into resistance from Republican senators in their home states after the midterm elections.

The White House on November 10 rescinded ​US District Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the ‌8th US Circuit Court of Appeals and nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland in his place following opposition ​from Arkansas' Republican senator. Hiland appeared at Wednesday's hearing with six other nominees.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston and ​David Morgan in Washington; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Alistair Bell)

articles.title: Ex-Penn State student faces federal charges after fraternity drug bust
articles.summary: A former Penn State University student was indicted on federal charges Wednesday for an alleged cocaine trafficking operation that authorities say he operated alongside more than a dozen other college students. The Justice Department (DOJ) announced charges against Agostino Abbatiello, a 24-year-old former Penn State student, who they allege sold cocaine in bulk to two…
articles.body:
A former Penn State University student was indicted on federal charges Wednesday for an alleged cocaine trafficking operation that authorities say he operated alongside more than a dozen other college students.

The Justice Department (DOJ) announced charges against Agostino Abbatiello, a 24-year-old former Penn State student, who they allege sold cocaine in bulk to two fraternities at the school and recruited others to help him transport it from suppliers in Philadelphia and New York.

Abbatiello is accused of using fraternity pledges and brothers from two fraternities — Delta Upsilon and Sigma Chi — to assist in the operation and prepare the cocaine for resale.

“College should be a marketplace of ideas and not illegal drugs,” U.S. Attorney Brian Miller said in the DOJ’s release. “Our office will continue working with the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s office, and with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and hold accountable those who profit from illegal drug activity in our communities.”

A total of 14 people were arrested in relation to the alleged trafficking operation in August, 13 of whom were or are still Penn State students, and one was one of their fathers.

Authorities previously alleged that the fraternities sold cocaine to students, primarily through Snapchat, and made hundreds of thousands of dollars in the process.

The maximum sentence for the charges is life in prison, according to the DOJ.

Penn State placed Delta Upsilon on an interim suspension after the university learned of the charges. The school already did not recognize Sigma Chi, and suspended the fraternity in 2021 for not following proper COVID-19 procedures, according to the Daily Collegian.

In 2024, fraternity alumni accused Penn State of unfair practices in its relationship with Greek organizations.

Federal authorities have a history of cracking down on fraternity drug trafficking operations. The DOJ charged 21 people across three North Carolina universities in 2020, and took the step of seizing three fraternity houses at the University of Virginia in 1991.

articles.title: Joe Biden reveals Nancy Pelosi force him out, exposed false polling
articles.summary: We can all appreciate a savvy political operator — even one who isn’t on my side.
articles.body:
Now, I may be completely opposed to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s policy agenda, but I can recognize a master at work. Even MAGA should respect how brutally effective she was at her job, which was defending and promoting the Democratic Party’s interests at all costs. Just look at how she handled former President Biden, ultimately forcing him from the race in 2024.

Even Biden is giving her some credit now. According to his new memoir, excerpts of which are appearing on social media, it was indeed Pelosi who really pushed him off stage.

In his memoir, titled “Promise Me, America,” Biden writes that he had always viewed Pelosi as a great friend, and appreciated that she was saying on television that it was Biden’s decision to make on whether to drop out following his disastrous debate performance. But privately, she told Biden directly that he needed to go.

Biden said: “She told me how great a president I had been. No one had gotten so much done. Then she told me how terrible my polling was and that I would be dragging her most vulnerable members down. She told me all the polling she had seen said I couldn’t win, but I could be the George Washington of our time if I passed the torch.”

Then Biden said they called it his pollster, Mike Donilon, who showed Pelosi numbers that showed a close and winnable race for Biden. Pelosi responded that she didn’t believe at all, that no credible poll showed Biden could win, and that if he didn’t go, the Democrats were going to get killed up and down the ballot.

And Pelosi got her wish — eventually Biden did withdraw from the race. His replacement, Kamala Harris, didn’t win either, but Democrats did better in the other races than they would have otherwise.

Our friend, The Hill’s Niall Stanage, writes on X : “Think whatever you like about her politics; she doesn’t mess about.”

In a review of the memoir itself, The Wall Street Journal’s Barton Swaim writes that the defining feature of Biden’s career is that he didn’t know when to run for president. He sat out 2016 when he would have been a better candidate than Hilary Clinton, and then he ran in 2024 when he obviously should have handed off the baton to his successor.

Pelosi convinced him to go because she told him he would be viewed as a George Washington-like figure. That was obviously not true, and I assume Pelosi knew it wasn’t true — it was far too late to salvage Biden’s reputation. But she was thinking of her party’s interests, and so she was happy to play on his need for praise.

Well done, former Madam Speaker! We can all appreciate a savvy political operator — even one who isn’t on my side.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Mullin defends taking government plane to LSU-Texas game after nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday he flew to a Saturday Louisiana State University college football game in part to not send a conflicting message one day after all flights in the United States were temporarily stopped. Mullin had previously said he did not want to disappoint his niece, who was…
articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday he flew to a Saturday Louisiana State University college football game in part to not send a conflicting message one day after all flights in the United States were temporarily stopped.

Mullin had previously said he did not want to disappoint his niece, who was eager to attend the game and has also noted he paid to cover his portion of the flight , given that he is mandated to travel on government aircraft.

But during a Wednesday appearance before a House panel, he also said he did not want the public to question the confidence of airline safety after the Friday groundstop was lifted.

“I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece who has never been to an LSU game and she’s a huge LSU game fan to a game. We had discussions at 10 o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it, and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace was completely open, it could bring confusion,” he told lawmakers while appearing before the House Homeland Security Committee.

“Because I was meeting the governor there, I was meeting other people there, that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly. There was a lot of stuff going on in the news saying, ‘Is it safe to fly?’ We were saying our skies are completely open. On Saturday alone, 36,000 planes flew and flew safely. Before I took off, the airspace had been open for almost 24 hours,” he said.

Like other national security officials, the DHS chief is required to travel by government plane and reimburse federal coffers an amount comparable to taking a commercial flight.

Mullin also said the team placed him in a suite at Tiger Stadium with a department contractor, saying he was unaware of that as he secured the tickets. One of the other attendees in that suite was Ben Bordelon, the CEO of Bollinger Shipping, which has some DHS contracts.

“They put us in the suite. I’d never met the company. I’d never met the team or the gentleman. I’d never had a conversation with them,” the secretary continued. “They’d been doing business with the United States Coast Guard for 40 years, well before DHS was even stood up.”

He was asked about the decision during an appearance on CNBC on Tuesday.

The department finalized a deal with Bollinger in July for icebreaker ships used by the Coast Guard, though the contract had initially been awarded in December 2025, before Mullin was secretary.

Mullin has come under criticism from some for going to the high-profile game between LSU and Texas at a time when many Americans were struggling with their connections because of the ground stoppage.

articles.body:
Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.), chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent letters to interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick Wednesday, asking them to appear before the panel as scrutiny into both grows in Washington.

Guthrie’s letter called on Kress, who’s been a top Nvidia executive for over a decade, to answer for whether the company helped Singaporean computing infrastructure firm Megaspeed evade U.S. export controls on sensitive AI chips.

“These reported events raise questions about the company’s compliance with existing federal law regarding the export of advanced technologies, as well as the robustness and efficacy of the company’s security controls,” the lawmaker wrote.

The request came after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia’s CEO post amid a public scandal surrounding his extramarital affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — whom U.S. intelligence believed was a spy for China.

Guthrie requested Kress appear for a briefing to explain Nvidia’s “internal controls and safeguards surrounding export compliance” before Dec. 2.

His other letter to Lutnick requested further information “regarding the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips.”

“The Committee seeks to further understand Commerce’s actions and how they align with broader U.S. national and economic security interests,” Guthrie wrote.

Along with Lutnick, Guthrie also requested Under Secretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler appear before the committee.

Nvidia and the Commerce Department did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

House Democrats are leading other probes into Lutnick’s family, asking they preserve business records related to Nvidia. Specifically, it called on the commerce secretary’s son, Brandon Lutnick, to hand over documents related to the investment firm for which he serves as CEO, Cantor Fitzgerald — which reportedly had dealings with Nvidia.

The secretary divested from the company before taking over the Commerce Department and gave control to his son, who also serves as its chair.

The letter was sent by the senior Democrats who are poised to chair the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.).

articles.body:
Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.) defeated Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.) to be the Democratic caucus vice chair in a highly contested race Wednesday.

Underwood won by a vote of 143-118. The Illinois Democrat co-chairs the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, which helps shape the party’s messaging strategy and develop talking points on key issues. She also serves on the House Appropriations Committee.

Jacobs, meanwhile, serves on the House Democratic Steering and Policy, Foreign Affairs and Armed Services committees. She has been a vocal progressive member of the conference, most notably advocating for a change in House rules to allow new parents in Congress to vote by proxy.

The Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) endorsed Underwood prior to the race, while the Congressional Progressive Caucus threw their support behind Jacobs.

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), who currently serves as vice chair of the Democratic Caucus, was elected as caucus chair in the next Congress.

The House also elected Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) as majority whip and Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) majority leader on Wednesday, as well as nominated House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to serve as Speaker.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.), a member of the CBC, told The Hill he has worked with Underwood on a number of projects.

“She’s been thorough. She started off in Congress on my committee, and she went over to the Appropriations Committee… And so I’ve worked with her. I have knowledge of her ability, and I’m proud of her skill set. But both of them are good. But you know, we had two good choices,” Thompson added.

articles.title: Trump administration urges Supreme Court to stop TPS for Venezuelans
articles.summary: The Trump administration urged the Supreme Court on Wednesday to stop temporary legal protections from being restored for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans, saying it would “foment chaos” and disregards the justices’ earlier commands. The Supreme Court last year twice ruled the administration could terminate Venezuelans’ Temporary Protected Status (TPS) as the litigation proceeds. Those decisions were technically temporary, however. Now, a lower court is set to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration urged the Supreme Court on Wednesday to stop temporary legal protections from being restored for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans, saying it would “foment chaos” and disregards the justices’ earlier commands.

The Supreme Court last year twice ruled the administration could terminate Venezuelans’ Temporary Protected Status (TPS) as the litigation proceeds.

Those decisions were technically temporary, however. Now, a lower court is set to effectively restore the program for Venezuela after Friday unless the justices intervene.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer warned it would force authorities to immediately release some 1,800 noncitizens from immigration detention and block ongoing deportation efforts.

“Giving effect to the district court’s order for even a moment at this late date will gravely harm the government, compelling it to release removable aliens into the country with no guarantee of ever successfully locating them and returning them to detention,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the justices.

“It will also cause mass confusion by requiring work authorizations for thousands of aliens to flip on and off as litigation progresses,” he added.

Created in 1990, TPS temporarily protects foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home countries because of armed conflict, natural disaster or other extraordinary conditions. It prevents deportation and provides recipients with a pathway to work authorization.

Trump has accused the Biden administration of abusing the program by expanding it to a total of 17 countries. Trump has looked to curtail it, spurring a wave of litigation from recipients and immigration groups who say he’s exceeding his authority and is acting out of racial animus.

The administration has emerged victorious at the Supreme Court multiple times before.

Last year, the court issued two temporary rulings that said Venezuelans’ protections could be cut off as litigation moved ahead. Then, the court took up the TPS battle on their regular docket — this time looking at Syria and Haiti — and ruled that at least most of the immigration groups’ arguments weren’t allowed.

The groups are still fighting, believing the court left the door open for them to still seek relief.

The Supreme Court formally handed back the Venezuela battle to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit earlier this month. The 9th Circuit has issued an order that would effectively restore Venezuelans’ status after Friday.

“The government is virtually certain to prevail on appeal, and allowing the injunction to go into effect at this late date will have disastrous consequences,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the court.

articles.title: White House counsel Will Scharf pushes back on Democrats’ mounting oversight demands
articles.summary: White House counsel Will Scharf on Wednesday effectively told incoming Democratic chairs to start over, arguing the executive is under no obligation to respond to letters as part of investigations launched by ranking members. The letter, broadly addressed to “ranking members” of the House and Senate, does not appear to have actually been delivered to…
articles.body:
White House counsel Will Scharf on Wednesday effectively told incoming Democratic chairs to start over, arguing the executive is under no obligation to respond to letters as part of investigations launched by ranking members.

The letter , broadly addressed to “ranking members” of the House and Senate, does not appear to have actually been delivered to committee leadership.

But it borrows from a practice used by President Trump in his first term and later former President Biden in arguing that the White House must only respond to demands from congressional majorities — a position Democrats won’t formally retake until January.

“Your demands do not reflect a request of the House, Senate, or a committee to which that body’s oversight authority has been delegated. As a result, Ranking Member requests in the 119th Congress do not trigger any obligation to ‘accommodate[e]… the needs of the conflicting branches.’ Although some of you may (or may not) become a Chair in the 120th Congress, that does not mean that requests from the 119th Congress carry over,” Scharf wrote.

“This should not be surprising to you given the Biden Administration took the same position in 2022,” he added.

In making his case, however, the attorney also cited an Office of Legal Counsel opinion drafted during Trump’s first term, when his administration bucked oversight requests from Democrats then in the minority.

“Another longstanding Executive Branch policy has been ‘to engage in the established process for accommodating congressional requests for information only when those requests come from a committee, subcommittee, or chairman authorized to conduct oversight.’…Individual members of Congress, including ranking minority members, do not have the authority to conduct oversight in the absence of a specific delegation by a full house, committee, or subcommittee,’” Scharf wrote referencing the 2017 opinion.

A spokeswomen for the House Judiciary Committee said they had not received it, writing that while “Mr. Sharf wrote a letter, it seems he didn’t bother to actually send it.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), set to chair that panel, cautioned those wrapped in coming investigations against heeding Scharf’s advice.

“We expect every person who receives a request from Congress—especially people who are government officials and whose salaries are paid for by the American taxpayers—to cooperate with our duly issued oversight inquiries,” he said in a statement.

“As the Supreme Court has repeatedly found, Congress has a broad constitutional responsibility and power to conduct oversight in order to legislate. We strongly suggest tuning out any third-party ‘advice’ to obstruct and defy Congress on the basis of specious legal theories.”

Democrats have already sent out numerous letters over their two years in the minority launching various probes into all manner of issues under the Trump administration, from his various construction projects , business ventures and the activities of his Cabinet members and families.

Earlier Wednesday, House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) sent a letter to a dozen figures associated with Trump, demanding they preserve documents and communications related to ongoing probes.

The letter is the second time this month that Scharf has pushed back on coming Democratic probes , though in both cases his correspondence appears to have been delivered to the media rather than the committees.

Last week Scharf argued that Democratic investigations could even be criminal in nature if done to harass the Trump family or their allies.

The investigative powers of Congress have largely been upheld by the courts, plus members are protected by the Speech and Debate Clause of the Constitution. Federal law also prohibits obstruction of a congressional investigation.

But Democrats have fired back that their work is underpinned by a legitimate legislative purpose.

“Our work is about taking on government corruption, making life more affordable through bringing down costs by actually going after the crooks and the criminals that are causing harm, and then writing good legislation to stop the corruption from happening in the future,” Garcia said last week during an appearance on MS NOW.

“And so, it’s outrageous that Donald Trump wants to stop any sort of oversight, and certainly he’s trying to stop us members of Congress from doing our job that is in the Constitution,” he said.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton dismisses Democratic leadership battle as a 'performance' as Schumer faces progressive revolt
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton called Sen. Chris Van Hollen's challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader a "performance."
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton dismissed the leadership challenge mounted by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., against Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate majority leader when Democrats take control in January as a "performance." During Clinton and co-host Kara Swisher's podcast, "High Stakes," Wednesday, Swisher asked the former secretary of state what she thought of Van Hollen's leadership challenge to Schumer. Clinton argued Democrats were elected because voters wanted changes in their own lives, not necessarily a change in Senate or House leadership. "So, this leadership battle, to me, is kind of performance, in a way," Clinton said. "Because if you think that the majority leader of the Senate is going to replace the voices of people like James Talarico or Abdul El-Sayed or Annie Andrews, you don't know what is going to happen in the Senate. "The majority leader will work to get legislation up, and he'll say, 'OK, Abdul, you want to put in Medicare-for-all, and Adam Hamilton, that's not your preferred approach. You work with the legislative team here to come up with your, and let's figure out how we're going to get something passed.'" DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES Van Hollen announced Nov. 12 that he would challenge Schumer, citing the midterm election results as a call for change. Earlier in the discussion, Clinton said the Senate leadership election should be an open process but argued that the majority leader wasn't really the "messenger." "I think anybody has a right to challenge the leadership of their party," she said. "I mean, it's — it should be an open process. And you know, I know Chris and have worked with him, but at this point, from my perspective, the majority leader is not the messenger. How many times did you see John Thune on television defending or espousing a message? "Their job is different," Clinton continued. "Their job is to push the committees, to mark up legislation, get it on the floor, get it passed, get it to the House, get it to the White House. "I want somebody who knows the ins and outs of the Senate," she said. "And just because you've been in the Senate doesn't mean that you have the, you know, hands-on experience or the team in place to really pull those parliamentary levers." Swisher asked, "So you think it's kind of performative?" Clinton said yes. Swisher also asked whether Schumer would survive the challenge from Van Hollen. "Yeah, I do," Clinton said. SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED Republican strategist Liz Mair told Fox News Digital, "The primary tasks of Senate majority leader are corralling votes to advance or stop legislation and literal vote counting to ensure the priorities of a caucus are advanced and agenda items they oppose are thwarted, with a healthy spoonful of good fundraising and steering of committee dollars to win tough races, something Schumer did pretty well this cycle. "His [Van Hollen's] campaign for leader apparently being all about supposed virtue signaling to the hard left on pet policies as opposed to his ability to perform the fundamentals of the job is why he's likely to lose this contest." Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade as both minority and majority leader, so far has 15 senators in his camp, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting. The longtime Democratic leader has remained confident, but quiet, about his chances of retaining his job, posting shortly after Van Hollen’s announcement last week that he welcomed "discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader." Van Hollen's base of support includes Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Senate Democrats; Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, both progressives whom Schumer did not initially back in their respective races. SCHUMER FACES MUTINY FROM NEWLY ELECTED SENATE DEMS AS PARTY PREPARES TO SEIZE POWER Van Hollen's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. articles.title: Mullin defends TSA shoes-on policy after congressman calls classified briefing ‘very concerning’
articles.summary: Markwayne Mullin defended the TSA shoe removal policy at a House Homeland Security hearing, telling Rep. Eli Crane the change never put anyone at risk.
articles.body: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended letting travelers keep their shoes on at airport checkpoints Wednesday after an Arizona congressman pressed him on why the TSA policy remains in place despite a classified watchdog review. "We have never put anyone at risk at all," Mullin told Rep. Eli Crane, R-Ariz., at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing. Mullin said the department evaluates screening technology daily and that he had personally met with DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari in a secure facility. "In fact, we addressed three of the four concerns," Mullin said. He said the fourth, in his view, had nothing to do with security. TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS Mullin gave no specifics about what DHS had done to address the three concerns or what the fourth involved. Crane said he had received a classified briefing from the inspector general and called it "very concerning." He asked Mullin to discuss the matter privately. The exchange put renewed scrutiny on a July 2025 decision by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to end routine shoe removal at TSA checkpoints nationwide. Noem said at the time that advances in screening technology would allow the agency to speed up lines while maintaining security. TSA officers could still ask travelers to remove their shoes for additional screening. Within weeks of the change, the inspector general sent DHS and TSA leaders a formal warning about a screening weakness, according to questions entered into the Senate record in July. WATCH: DEM SCOLDS HOMELAND SECURITY CHIEF TO ‘CALM DOWN’ AFTER HEARING DERAILS OVER ALLEGED ‘PATTERN’ The watchdog issued its final classified report on Nov. 1, 2025. In a March memo reviewed by CBS News, Cuffari said his office was still waiting for the agencies’ formal response after the 90-day deadline had passed. The Senate record also shows that Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., asked TSA in April to reverse the policy until the screening weakness was addressed. In a May response cited by Cantwell, then-acting TSA Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill said "current intelligence and risk assessments indicate no direct, credible threats related to shoes." articles.title: Britt proposes creating national office to address financial fraud
articles.summary: GOP Sen. Katie Britt (Ala.) on Wednesday introduced legislation to create a national office dedicated to fighting financial fraud and scams. Britt’s bill proposes forming a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention within the White House. That bureau would develop a “comprehensive national strategy and strengthen coordination” among federal agencies, financial institutions and technology…
articles.body:
GOP Sen. Katie Britt (Ala.) on Wednesday introduced legislation to create a national office dedicated to fighting financial fraud and scams .

Britt’s bill proposes forming a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention within the White House.

That bureau would develop a “comprehensive national strategy and strengthen coordination” among federal agencies, financial institutions and technology companies on preventing frauds and scams, Britt’s office said .

The proposed office would also promote timely intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors and improve assistance for victims of financial fraud.

Individuals reported losing $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) reported in June . That marks a nearly threefold increase since 2020, the FTC noted.

Britt said Wednesday that Americans “should not have to worry that one fraudulent call, text, or online message could cost them their life savings,” adding the federal government needs a “coordinated approach” to the problem.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” the Alabama Republican added in a statement.

“When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

Britt’s legislation has the backing of top industry groups, including the American Bankers Association, the Community Bankers of America and the Financial Services Forum.

Nearly three-fourths of American adults the Pew Research Center surveyed last year said they had experienced an online scam or attack, such as a credit card fraud or shopping scams.

Britt, a member of the Senate Appropriations and Banking panels, has also co-sponsored legislation that would allow state, local and tribal authorities to use federal grant funds to crack down on scams directed at the elderly.

The House passed the bipartisan GUARD Act in September, sending it to the upper chamber. Senators are scheduled to be in session this week and during the first three weeks of December, before their annual holiday recess.

articles.title: New York presses ICE on winter safety at tent facility for women
articles.summary: The state of New York pressed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) about winter safety at a Batavia detention center for women in a letter sent on Tuesday. New York’s Department of Health (DOH) and Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) wrote to ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall that they were pursuing “information relating to Akima Infrastructure…
articles.body:
The state of New York pressed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) about winter safety at a Batavia detention center for women in a letter sent on Tuesday.

New York’s Department of Health (DOH) and Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) wrote to ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall that they were pursuing “information relating to Akima Infrastructure Protection LLC (Akima)’s construction and anticipated operation of a tent detention facility on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at the Buffalo Service Processing Center (BSPC).”

“To date, DEC and DOH have not received any information or outreach from the federal government or Akima about this facility,” DEC Commissioner Amanda Lefton and DOH Commissioner of Health James McDonald wrote.

“We understand from public reporting, however, that the facility may be used to detain up to 100 women and will employ numerous staff,” the two officials added.

In October, local outlet the Times Union reported that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was going ahead with an expansion of the Buffalo (Batavia) Service Processing Center.

According to the Times Union, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Rep. Timothy Kennedy (D-N.Y.) in a September letter that the expansion was occurring.

Mullin also told Kennedy that the expansion at the ICE facility would hold female detainees, the outlet said.

“We understand that Akima has entered into a contract with ICE and/or DHS to construct and operate a ‘temporary detention structure’ to house up to 100 female detainees of all security levels,” Lefton and McDonald wrote in their letter. “Public contracting documents indicate that the facility will be ‘soft sided’ and will be located adjacent to where the Batavia Service Processing Center is located,”

“The construction and maintenance of a safe and environmentally sound tentbased residential or institutional facility can be difficult. Severe weather, including extended subfreezing temperatures and winter storms, can present additional challenges,” they added.

An ICE spokesperson told The Hill on Wednesday that “It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and is actively working to expand detention space.”

The Hill has reached out to Akima for comment.
