articles.title: Mullin, Clayton face bipartisan grilling over tech outages
articles.summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said there was no evidence that tech outages hitting businesses across the country were the result of nefarious actions at a timely hearing Wednesday on worldwide threats facing the country. The series of tech disruptions, including communications failures that led to a Friday…
articles.body:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said there was no evidence that tech outages hitting businesses across the country were the result of nefarious actions at a timely hearing Wednesday on worldwide threats facing the country.

The series of tech disruptions, including communications failures that led to a Friday ground stop from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), have fueled questions from the public about whether there is reason for worry.

Fears have also been sparked by reports that Iran is developing plans to set off a dirty bomb in Washington.

Clayton said he understood why people were worried, and why it was raising questions.

“The American people should ask us these questions,” he told the House Homeland Security Committee. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

“They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton said.

That answer was not fully satisfying to several Republicans as well as Democrats who expressed skepticism there was not a connection linking the various incidents.

“I’m getting a lot of text messages, phone calls about these issues, and I think one of the concerns is how quickly and how many of these outages we’ve seen … in a span of five days, when we’ve never seen that,” said Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.).

Rep. Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.) asked Clayton if he believes in coincidences.

“I believe in exploring coincidences,” Clayton responded.

It was, LaLota acknowledged, a “good answer,” but the lawmaker said he still has concerns.

“I’m a little worried that what’s happened this last week are a little beyond coincidences,” he stated.

“Thursday, Microsoft 365 went down. Friday, a nationwide ground stop. Monday, United Airlines grounded flights. Also Monday, Chase and Wells Fargo experienced banking disruptions. And yesterday, we learned of a network disruption at the NSA [National Security Agency]. Five major disruptions in less than a week. Five different explanations,” he said, later asking Clayton if his “gut” tells him they still are a coincidence.

“It does, and let me tell you why,” Clayton responded. “It’s an informed opinion, and the reason it’s informed is we are engaged in a substantial increase in upgrades, the number of patches, the number of upgrades that we’re undertaking in the public and private,” Clayton said before explaining the review done by the government.

“We call it red teaming. We say, OK, let’s say we wanted to do this and not be detected, and make it look like it wasn’t coordinated, and try to establish all of that. That’s the kind of exercise that our experts at the FBI and the like will go on,” he said.

Democrats were quick to highlight President Trump’s response.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (Miss.), the top Democrat on the panel, held up a sign with a quote from Trump, who — when asked about the ground stop — said, “I don’t take any responsibility.”

Many Democrats cited the gutting of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), which faced widespread firings under Trump and plays a critical role in battling tech vulnerabilities.

“All three of your agencies — perhaps not Mr. Clayton — have decimated the cybersecurity personnel that this administration entered office with. CISA is way down because the president didn’t want election fraud to be uncovered. The FBI has fired numerous cybersecurity agents because they may or may not have served a subpoena in the Mar-a-Lago case. You all have an obligation to restore that,” Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.) said.

Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) noted that CISA had 3,400 employees at the start of the Trump administration and pointed to June testimony from Mullin saying the agency was down to 2,200 employees but really needed 2,800.

“Let’s be clear about what happened. The Trump administration inherited a CISA workforce of 3,400 people. They fired and pushed out — more than 1,000 cyber defenders — at precisely the moment the cyber threat was exploding. You came before us and said correctly that you needed hundreds of those employees back,” Walkinshaw said.

“So I have a simple question for you: Was it a mistake in 2025 for those employees, the 1,000-plus CISA employees that you now need back? Was it a mistake for them to have been fired and pushed out?”

Mullin wouldn’t say that it was, saying it happened before his arrival.

“I didn’t say [we needed] those employees back. I said we’re hiring new people,” he countered.

The focus on cyber issues overshadowed other major developments that represent potential threats to the nation.

There were just a handful of questions about Iran’s plans for a “dirty bomb.”

Mullin said he did not believe Iran’s exploration of such a weapon constituted an imminent threat.

Clayton wouldn’t get into specifics but did repeatedly highlight the risk posed by Iran in his opening remarks and responses to questions.

“We do face a heightened threat from the Iranians – lethal plotting against our citizens at home and abroad,” he said.

Mullin did face several questions about immigration matters from both Democrats and Republicans during the hearing.

Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.), a Cuban-born lawmaker in a heavily Hispanic district, told Mullin he thought the administration had strayed from going after criminals saying, “I just think you’ve gone a little bit too far.”

Roughly 70 percent of those in immigration detention have no criminal record, but Mullin asserted they did, even as the administration has come under fire for detaining those with lawful immigration status.

“Our policy right now is to go after the worst, the worst. But every time you go out for the worst, the worst, you also have what we call collateral criminals. So when we arrest someone that’s on a warrant, most of the time they’re not by themselves. There’ll be two or three individuals with them,” Mullin said.

He was later asked by Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) if Mullin had “any regrets or reservations for the leading role you are playing in this administration’s immigration agenda” later added “about even killing people.”

Mullin disputed that he had, saying “We’re not killing people.”

That prompted Mullin to respond, “That’s your opinion.”

“No, no, you are killing people. The whole entire country watches you kill people,” McIver said as her time for questions ended.

FBI Director Kash Patel skipped the hearing and sent his deputy, bucking a decadelong tradition and garnering a stern rebuke from House Homeland Security Chair Andrew Garbarino (R-N.Y.).

Patel was roasted in absentia by members of both parties for his failure to appear.

“Today’s hearing date was first provided to Director Patel in August. There was no surprise or last-minute request, and despite repeated attempts over the span of several months between then and now to find any date when he could testify, the director made clear that he had no intention of appearing,” Garbarino said in his opening remarks.

“Director Patel’s refusal to testify marks a significant departure from well-established committee precedent.”

An FBI official said Patel was traveling to field offices this week.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries’ progressive defectors reveal the limits of their power: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Seven incoming members of the House Democratic Caucus made their first big move since winning their elections this month, publicly stating that they voted against Hakeem Jeffries’ nomination to be the next speaker after a secret-ballot contest today.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into Hakeem Jeffries’ big win on Capitol Hill. Plus, Lawrence Hurley explains why President Donald Trump’s legal battles with Congress could stretch on long after he exits the White House. — Adam Wollner Hakeem Jeffries’ progressive defectors reveal the limits of their power Analysis by Jonathan Allen Seven incoming members of the House Democratic Caucus made their first big move since winning their elections this month, publicly stating that they voted against Hakeem Jeffries’ nomination to be the next speaker after a secret-ballot contest today. Jeffries, who led his party to a historic rout of Republicans in November, faced no opponent. That made the fringe of his party, especially the progressive, online flank, angry. He was too moderate, too sympathetic to Israel, too accommodating to lead Democrats in the House, they argued. Four others joined the recalcitrant in voting against his nomination. Jeffries pushed back, not with words, but with votes: 251 of them. If he gets the same tally on the House floor in January, it will be only the second time since the 1994 “Republican Revolution” that a candidate for speaker has eclipsed 250 votes and the first time since retiring Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., picked up 255 votes in 2009. Either way, he will make history as the first Black speaker of the House. The “Stubborn Seven” — Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York; Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania; Adam Hamawy of New Jersey; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Frederick Haynes of Texas — cast what some lawmakers call “hero” votes. That is, they decided to risk retribution from party leaders, and ostracism by their peers, in order to flex muscle for a national constituency of the far left. All but Hamawy and Haynes are members of the Democratic Socialists of America. The seven wrote in a statement that they have “worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations” on issues including “Medicare for All” and ending the war in the Gaza Strip. “While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they continued. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.” But if they were seeking to create leverage, their gambit backfired. Archimedes purportedly said that if given a place to stand and a lever, he could move the world. By taking their stand, these seven Democrats risk kneecapping themselves with the lever. Now, it’s clear that Jeffries doesn’t need their votes. He could lose 33 more and still win the speaker’s gavel next year. He may never need them for anything. Perhaps he will choose to be magnanimous and refrain from punishing them. But he may also not go out of his way to help them. It is the speaker who decides which House members can use public funds for congressional delegation trips abroad. It is the speaker who controls the internal panel that picks committee assignments. As one former House Democratic chief of staff said in an interview today, Jeffries could decide to resurrect a long-since-disbanded backwater panel — the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service — and stock it with the seven freshmen who voted against him. Then again, they may have inadvertently done Jeffries a favor: They showed the rest of their caucus, and the party’s voters, just how strong of a position he will be in at the start of his speakership. 🏛️ More from the Hill: Newly elected House Democrats met today with former President Barack Obama. Read more → Trump’s legal fight against congressional investigations could outlast his presidency By Lawrence Hurley When Democrats issued subpoenas in 2019 seeking information about President Donald Trump’s finances, it prompted a furious legal fight that wasn’t resolved until after he left office at the end of his first term. The House Oversight and Reform Committee ended up getting some of the information it sought from the accounting firm Mazars in 2022, during the Biden administration, but by then the political value of it had receded. The same happened with attempts by Democrats to obtain Trump’s tax records, which were finally disclosed in late 2022 after the Supreme Court declined to intervene. With Democrats now about to take control of Congress and vowing to launch a new wave of investigations on issues ranging from the Trump family businesses to immigration enforcement, history could repeat itself. The Trump administration has already pledged to fight requests for information, even launching its own threats to prosecute members of Congress for mounting unwarranted investigations, despite legal immunity lawmakers have under the Constitution. “If you delay enough, people move on to the next outrage,” said Emily Berman, an expert on executive power at the University of Houston Law Center. Read more → ➡️ Related: U.S. attorney demands Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff preserve communications related to Trump oversight, by Ryan J. Reilly That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who was nominated earlier Wednesday to serve as Speaker next term, will have a “hard time” keeping the Democrats together.

“He’s going to have a hard time keeping his conference together, that’s my prediction,” Johnson told a TMZ DC reporter .

When the reporter asked if he thinks Jefferies will do a good job, Johnson responded by saying, “Of course. Hakeem’s a friend, colleague. The American people need Congress to work. I just think it’s going to be a great challenge for him to do that.”

On Wednesday, House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Jeffries in a 251-11 vote to be the next House Speaker. This is the first step in a two-step process which will be completed with a full House vote on Jan. 3.

The New York Democrat, who ran uncontested, will need 218 votes on the chamber floor in January to secure his position. If he succeeds in getting the required number of votes, Jeffries will be the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.

While Jeffries managed to get a majority of the support from his party, there were some who did not back him.

A group of seven incoming House Democrats, who were among the 11 who voted against Jeffries, issued a joint statement to let their votes be known to the public. The group includes Rep.-elects Darializa Avila Chevalier (N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (N.J.), Frederick Haynes (Texas), Melat Kiros (Colo.), Donavan McKinney (Mich.), Chris Rabb (Pa.) and Claire Valdez (N.Y.).

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” the statement read.

A spokesperson for Haynes said in a statement shared with Time that he “woke up unexpectedly ill this morning” and “narrowly missed the vote.” His team noted that if he did cast his vote, it would have been against Jeffries becoming House Speaker.

articles.title: Dozens of Army soldiers sign up for unique reenlistment incentive to play Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.summary: The U.S. Army offered Fort Stewart soldiers four-day passes to play "Grand Theft Auto VI" as a reenlistment perk, and 43 of 130 eligible troops took it.
articles.body: The U.S. Army turned to one of the year’s most anticipated video games to get soldiers at Fort Stewart, Georgia, talking about reenlisting. The offer was a four-day pass to play "Grand Theft Auto VI" when it launches Thursday. The Army said 43 of the 130 eligible soldiers in the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion chose the perk when they reenlisted for two to six more years, Task & Purpose first reported. NBA PLAYER PREDICTS AMERICAN ATHLETES' PERFORMANCES WILL DIP IN NOVEMBER WHILE THEY PLAY GTA "I’m all campaign. I’m all about the heist," Sgt. Jamire Smith, a combat engineer who signed up for six more years in the Army and took the four-day pass, told Task & Purpose. "I think I have a good 24 hours to waste on it." Smith said he had been close to leaving the Army before leaders in his company and battalion showed him they still needed his skills. He qualified for a roughly $60,000 reenlistment bonus after training to drive heavy breaching vehicles, the outlet reported. US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT The battalion offered the pass from Aug. 1 through Nov. 14. The Army said the time off came on top of standard reenlistment incentives, which can include cash bonuses or a choice of duty station depending on a soldier’s eligibility and the Army’s needs. Staff Sgt. Brittany Wolfer, the battalion’s career counselor, called the perk an "eye grabber." She pitched it to her commander after hearing Sgt. Maj. Celeste R. Spencer, a senior Army career counselor, float the idea on TikTok. Wolfer said the battalion had gone about eight months without a career counselor before she arrived, and she wanted soldiers nearing a decision about reenlisting to know whom to talk to about their options. The commander had played "Grand Theft Auto 2" and backed the idea, Wolfer told the outlet. Wolfer, a gamer herself, went to basic training the same week "Grand Theft Auto V" came out. Staff Sgt. Floyd Maxwell, a network systems and communications specialist, signed up for three more years. He told the outlet his father, who died a few months ago, had encouraged him to make a career of the Army. He said the battalion had also given him a sense of family. "The excitement from this incentive has sparked positive conversations amongst Soldiers to discuss the continuation of their service in the Army," the Army said in a statement. The service said it recognized the 3rd Infantry Division as its top division for retention in 2025. MIAMI HEAT FINALLY UNVEIL 'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI'-THEMED JERSEYS AND SOCIAL MEDIA IS LOVING THEM The game has an Army connection of its own. One of its main characters, Jason Duval, served in the Army before going to work for drug runners in the Florida Keys, according to Rockstar Games. Wolfer had a suggestion for the studio, too. She wants it to put Rocky the Bulldog, the 3rd Infantry Division’s mascot, in the game. "Grand Theft Auto VI" had already brought in an estimated $1.65 billion from more than 17 million preorders by Wednesday, Forbes reported, citing market research firm Sensor Tower. MIAMI HEAT UNVEIL VICE CITY COURT FOR 'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI'-THEMED CLASH WITH MILWAUKEE BUCKS Hours before the U.S. launch, PlayStation warned that a network disruption could make it difficult for some players to launch games or access online features. Its status page showed the issue was resolved by 2:30 p.m. ET, Axios reported. Rockstar says the game unlocks at midnight local time Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the Army for comment. Fox News' Liz Friden contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russian national who targeted Palantir workers charged as a foreign agent, sources say
articles.summary: Igor D’iu bought laptops, remote access software and cellphones, then sat at a Palo Alto coffee shop near Palantir’s headquarters, according to an affidavit.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A Russian national accused of sneaking into the U.S. over the summer to spy on employees at the tech giant Palantir has been indicted on charges of conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government, fraud and stalking, according to two people familiar with the investigation. Igor D’iu bought laptops, remote access software and cellphones, then sat at a coffee shop in Palo Alto, California, just a three-minute walk from Palantir, which builds tools used by both private companies and the Pentagon, according to a court-filed affidavit. At the coffee shop, D’iu photographed laptop screens of employees as they worked there, the Justice Department said in a statement Wednesday. The court documents contain images taken by the alleged spy showing a Palantir employee sitting in the shade of a busy outdoor patio, laptop open. He was instructed to position his laptop near the company so his co-conspirators could remotely access data, federal prosecutors said. When D’iu asked his handlers who he was working for, he was told “the Motherland,” according to the court documents. The company is not named in the indictment. Two people familiar with the arrest told NBC News it was Palantir. Bloomberg News first reported that Palantir employees were the alleged target. The company did not immediately return emails seeking comment Wednesday. It wasn’t immediately clear whether D’iu had an attorney yet who could comment on the charges against him. Over the past few weeks, allegations of spying have rocketed through the tech world: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after reports that he had extramarital relationships, including one with a woman believed to be spying for China. Huang has said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life. Last month, a former OpenAI engineer, a Saudi national, was accused of planting a listening device at the company. He has said he’s not guilty. News of D’iu’s indictment also comes hours before President Donald Trump is set to meet one-on-one with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of a summit in China. FBI Director Kash Patel said last week that his agency had made 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests since Trump started his second term. He said it was a 53% increase from the same 21 months of the Biden administration. “I want to send a clear message — this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” he posted on X. The allegations against D’iu come as both Ukraine and Russia push to gain a technological advantage on the battlefield, including through the growing use of AI. The two countries have been building out their capabilities, but experts say Ukraine’s advantage is, in part, its access to Western technology Russia has been shut out from. Palantir has been a close ally of Ukraine in its war with Russia following a full-scale invasion in February 2022. It was among the first major U.S. tech companies to offer help to the embattled nation, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hosted Palantir CEO Alex Karp in Kyiv this past May. The two discussed technological development, Zelenskyy said in a statement at the time. “Step by step, we are developing cooperation with the American defense sector,” he said. “Palantir is a renowned global company with strong potential, and there certainly are areas where we can be useful to one another, strengthening the defense of Ukraine, America, and our partners.” “We refused to work in Russia and China, even though that cost us money,” said Louis Mosley, Palantir’s executive vice president in the U.K. and Europe, in a September social media post. “We went into Kyiv in May 2022 and stayed. We did both because of what we believe, not what we could sell.” Mosley has regularly traveled to Ukraine since the beginning of the war and worked with government initiatives building out the battlefield technology sector. Karp has also been in contact with Mykhaivo Fedorov, the ousted Ukrainian defense minister who was known for the technological innovations he pushed forward. In a news conference following his dismissal, Fedorov said Karp called him to offer a job. The two men met when Fedorov traveled to the U.S. this fall. Karp became the first investor in a new defense company Fedorov subsequently launched. According to the affidavit, D’iu stalked several Palantir employees, following at least one home from work. The employee noticed a man in a silver Lexus following her from the office for nearly 30 miles, running a red light, making illegal turns and turning onto back roads to stay on her tail, according to court documents. She flagged a San Francisco police officer down and reported the incident. Palantir identified the vehicle using security footage from its campus, and police tracked down D’iu and asked him what he was doing. “He said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was beautiful. D’iu told officers he followed the woman because he wanted to ask her out on a date,” according to court papers. He said he was in the U.S. on a tourist visa, but federal prosecutors say he traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, and illegally crossed the U.S.-Mexico border. Prosecutors said he received more and more assignments from his handlers and received fake documents in order to stay in the U.S. The FBI said it searched his home and recovered a notebook with 10 addresses of company employees and detailed profiles of at least three of them, including their family members’ names and employment and educational histories.

articles.title: High school valedictorians to get Nike shoes after request from Mississippi’s incoming senator
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s taste in footwear may have just added a new incentive for high school seniors to keep up their grades.
articles.body: Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s taste in footwear may have just added a new incentive for high school seniors to keep up their grades. This week, the incoming Mississippi senator convinced Nike to present Mississippi high school valedictorians with custom Air Force 1 sneakers. Nike then expanded his pledge to valedictorians across the U.S. “@Nike & @nikestore to honor this moment in Mississippi history, how about custom-made AF1s (my fav shoe) for every valedictorian of Mississippi high school this year?” Colom wrote in a post on X Monday. “It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit” Colom, a Democrat, is set to take office next year as the first Black senator for Mississippi since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. He will also be the first Democrat to represent the state since John Stennis left office in 1989. Colom doubled down on the request to Nike on Wednesday, enlisting Joe Holder, a columnist and Nike Master Trainer, to help convince the brand to support the cause. “@JoeHolder_ help us get @Nike to do the right thing,” Colom wrote. “It’s a historic moment that we can leverage to help motivate MS kids to hit the books!” Nike responded Thursday, writing in a post on X, “The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea.” Expanding on Colom’s original request to send shoes to valedictorians in Mississippi, Nike said it would send the shoes nationwide. “@scott_colom, we’ll do you one better… For this year, 2026/2027 high school valedictorians from across the U.S., let’s go!” the company wrote, adding, “Stay tuned for more info.” Nike has not announced what the shoe will look like, but Colom responded to its post with a suggestion that the design honor Hiram Revels, the first Black member of Congress. Revels took office in 1870, representing Mississippi in the Senate, and advocated for civil rights and the desegregation of American schools and railroads. “I’m so proud of @Nike for stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment,” Colom said in a post celebrating Nike’s announcement. “This is the #justdoit mentality that makes your company great.” Colom, who was often spotted wearing a pair of Nike Air Force 1s on the campaign trail, spent time on college campuses to motivate young voters to get to the polls ahead of the midterm election. He also gave his victory speech on Nov. 11 at Tougaloo College in Jackson, Mississippi, with a group of college students standing behind him. After the election, Colom thanked college students and young voters for helping clinch his win, visiting Tougaloo, Jackson State University and his alma mater, Millsaps College, to celebrate with students.
